title: Right effort
hookLine: four efforts: to prevent, to abandon, to arouse, to maintain (AN 4.13)
last: ENOUGH — CONTENTMENT IS THE BEST RICHES.

cards: Anyone who has kept a garden knows there are four jobs. Keep weed seeds from blowing in. Pull the weeds that have already come up.
Plant what you want to grow. And water what's already growing, so it doesn't wilt. Skip any one, and the garden suffers, however hard you work at the other three.
The Buddha gave the sixth factor of his path the same four-part shape: two jobs about the harmful, two about the good.

teach.b: Sammā vāyāma. Vāyāma means effort, exertion, striving. In the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha lays out four right strivings.
For unwholesome states that haven't arisen: work so they don't arise.
For unwholesome states that have arisen: work to let them go. For wholesome states that haven't arisen: work to bring them about.
For wholesome states that have arisen: work to keep them from fading, and help them grow to fullness. The next sutta gives them short names: restraint, abandoning, developing, protecting.

Each uses the same string of verbs: you generate desire, make an effort, rouse energy, apply your mind, and strive. Desire is in there on purpose; the wish to do good is part of the engine. Two things about the shape.

teach.h: HALF OF IT IS ABOUT THE GOOD.
teach.b: It's balanced: half of right effort is about growing and keeping the good, and people new to practice often pour everything into the first two and forget the gardener's last two jobs.
And each asks for a different kind of effort. Preventing is quiet, like latching a gate. Abandoning is active, like pulling a weed.
Arousing takes initiative, like planting. Maintaining takes patience, like daily watering. So the question isn't only am I trying hard enough.

teach.h: WHICH ONE DOES THIS MOMENT NEED?
teach.b: It's which of the four this moment needs.
The next four days take them one at a time.

how: Buddhist teachers often present right effort through the four right strivings, and practitioners use them to decide what a moment of practice needs: restraint, letting go, cultivating, or sustaining.

o: straining until the body can bear no more
always pushing to win at work and in sport
right effort: four ways of working with the mind

games.q: the four efforts: tap the pairs.
p: letting go of what has arisen

s: right effort means trying as hard as possible at everything
it's four specific efforts, and each moment needs a different one.
half of right effort is about growing and keeping the good
the third and fourth efforts arouse and maintain wholesome states.
desire has no place in right effort
the formula begins: one generates desire, then makes an effort.

games.q: you snapped at someone an hour ago, and resentment is still simmering. which of the four efforts fits this moment?
games.why: the resentment has already arisen, so the second effort, abandoning, fits; preventing is for what hasn't come up yet.

practice: Let your mind walk the last day like a gardener walking the rows: something unhelpful you can see coming, something already sprouting that needs pulling, something good to plant, something good already growing that needs water.
Don't fix anything; choose one of the four, and let your attention rest there with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sammā vāyāma. Right effort: prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain. The sixth factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali sammā vāyāma: right effort, the sixth factor of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: four efforts. Prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain: two for the harmful, two for the good. Day three hundred eighty-three, done.
